# Example: Bucket Owner Granting Cross-Account Bucket Permissions

Granting permissions to IAM roles is a better practice than granting permissions to individual users. That said, this example walks through the user-based case. An AWS account such as Account A can grant another AWS account, Account B, permission to access its resources, such as buckets and objects. Account B can then delegate the permissions it receives from Account A to users in its own account. Account A can also directly grant a user in Account B permissions by using a bucket policy. Even so, a user in Account B still needs permission from the parent account, Account B, even if Account B doesn't have permissions from Account A. As long as the user has permission from both the resource owner and the parent account, the user will be able to access the resource.

## How the walkthrough works

The Account A administrator user attaches a bucket policy granting cross-account permissions to Account B to perform specific bucket operations. The administrator user in Account B automatically inherits the permissions granted to Account B. The Account B administrator user then attaches a user policy to the user, delegating the permissions it received from Account A. Finally, the user in Account B verifies permissions by accessing an object in the bucket owned by Account A.

## Setup

The walkthrough does not use root user credentials. Instead, an administrator user is created in each account and used to create resources and grant permissions. Account A has AWS account ID 1111-1111-1111 and administrator user AccountAadmin; Account B has AWS account ID 2222-2222-2222 and administrator user AccountBadmin.

Creating users and granting permissions is done in the AWS Management Console. Permissions are verified using the AWS CLI or AWS Tools for Windows PowerShell, so no code needs to be written. AccountAadmin is granted administrator privileges by attaching a user policy giving full access. All users in an account must use the account's IAM user sign-in URL when signing in to the AWS Management Console. With the AWS CLI, two profiles, AccountAadmin and AccountBadmin, are created for the administrator users' credentials.

## Step 1: Account A grants permissions

AccountAadmin signs in to the console, creates the bucket amzn-s3-demo-bucket, and attaches a policy to it. The bucket policy grants Account B the s3:GetLifecycleConfiguration and s3:ListBucket permissions on amzn-s3-demo-bucket. After the bucket policy is attached, Account B (and thus its administrator user) can perform s3:ListBucket and s3:GetLifecycleConfiguration on the bucket.

## Step 2: Account B delegates to a user

The Account B administrator creates user Dave in Account B. An inline policy attached to Dave allows only the s3:ListBucket action on amzn-s3-demo-bucket.

## Step 3: Verify permissions

Dave in Account B can list the contents of amzn-s3-demo-bucket owned by Account A. Dave doesn't have any permissions other than s3:ListBucket, so if Dave tries get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration, Amazon S3 returns permission denied.

## Step 4: Explicit deny (optional check)

Permissions can be granted by using an ACL, a bucket policy, or a user policy. However, an explicit deny set by either a bucket policy or a user policy takes precedence over any other permissions. If the bucket policy explicitly denies Account B the s3:ListBucket permission, Account B and users in Account B will not be able to list objects in amzn-s3-demo-bucket. After the explicit deny policy replaces the bucket policy, AccountBadmin's attempt to get a bucket list is denied access.

## Cleanup

For cleanup, the bucket policy is removed from amzn-s3-demo-bucket, and the objects and then the bucket are deleted if the bucket was created for this exercise. The AccountAadmin and AccountBadmin users are also deleted.

# Cross-account bucket permissions: delegating access to a user in another account

An AWS account such as Account A can grant another AWS account, Account B, permission to access its resources, such as buckets and objects. That grant alone is enough for Account B to delegate the permissions it receives from Account A to users in its own account. Account A can also grant a user in Account B permissions directly by using a bucket policy. Even so, a user in Account B still needs permission from the parent account, Account B, even if Account B itself doesn't have permissions from Account A. As long as the user has permission from both the resource owner and the parent account, the user will be able to access the resource. Granting permissions to IAM roles is a better practice than granting permissions to individual users. Permissions can be granted by using an ACL, a bucket policy, or a user policy.

## Overview of the walkthrough

The Account A administrator user attaches a bucket policy granting cross-account permissions to Account B to perform specific bucket operations. The administrator user in Account B automatically inherits the permissions granted to Account B. The Account B administrator user then attaches a user policy to the user, delegating the permissions it received from Account A. Finally, the user in Account B verifies permissions by accessing an object in the bucket owned by Account A. Each step must happen in this order: the bucket policy comes before the user policy, and the user policy comes before verification.

## Setup

The walkthrough does not use root user credentials. Instead, an administrator user is created in each account and used to create resources and grant permissions. Account A has AWS account ID 1111-1111-1111 and administrator user AccountAadmin; Account B has AWS account ID 2222-2222-2222 and administrator user AccountBadmin.

Creating users and granting permissions is done in the AWS Management Console. Permissions are verified using the AWS CLI or AWS Tools for Windows PowerShell, so no code needs to be written. AccountAadmin is granted administrator privileges by attaching a user policy giving full access. All users in an account must use the account's IAM user sign-in URL when signing in to the AWS Management Console. With the AWS CLI, two profiles, AccountAadmin and AccountBadmin, are created for the administrator users' credentials.

## Step 1: Create the bucket and attach a bucket policy in Account A

AccountAadmin signs in to the console and creates the bucket amzn-s3-demo-bucket and attaches a policy to it. This must happen before the policy's permissions take effect. The bucket policy grants Account B the s3:GetLifecycleConfiguration and s3:ListBucket permissions on amzn-s3-demo-bucket. After the bucket policy is attached, Account B (and thus its administrator user) can perform s3:ListBucket and s3:GetLifecycleConfiguration on the bucket.

## Step 2: Create a user and delegate permissions in Account B

Once the bucket policy has been attached, the Account B administrator creates user Dave in Account B. After Dave exists, an inline policy is attached to Dave that allows only the s3:ListBucket action on amzn-s3-demo-bucket.

## Step 3: Verify permissions

Dave in Account B can list the contents of amzn-s3-demo-bucket owned by Account A, but only because both conditions hold: the bucket policy grants Account B the permission, and Dave's inline policy allows s3:ListBucket. Dave doesn't have any permissions other than s3:ListBucket. If Dave tries get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration, Amazon S3 returns permission denied.

An explicit deny set by either a bucket policy or a user policy takes precedence over any other permissions. If the bucket policy explicitly denies Account B the s3:ListBucket permission, Account B and users in Account B will not be able to list objects in amzn-s3-demo-bucket. This cannot be true at the same time as Account B being able to perform s3:ListBucket after the original bucket policy is attached. After the explicit deny policy replaces the bucket policy, AccountBadmin's attempt to get a bucket list is denied access.

For cleanup, the bucket policy is removed from amzn-s3-demo-bucket, and the objects and then the bucket are deleted if the bucket was created for this exercise. The AccountAadmin and AccountBadmin users are also deleted.

# Cross-Account Bucket Permissions Walkthrough

## Concepts

Granting permissions to IAM roles is a better practice than granting permissions to individual users. Even so, this walkthrough delegates to a user to illustrate the mechanics.

An AWS account such as Account A can grant another AWS account, Account B, permission to access its resources, such as buckets and objects. Account B can then delegate the permissions it receives from Account A to users in its own account. Account A can also directly grant a user in Account B permissions using a bucket policy.

Access depends on two sources of permission. A user in Account B still needs permission from the parent account, Account B, even if Account B doesn't have permissions from Account A. As long as the user has permission from both the resource owner and the parent account, the user will be able to access the resource.

Permissions can be granted by using an ACL, a bucket policy, or a user policy. An explicit deny set by either a bucket policy or a user policy takes precedence over any other permissions.

## Overview of the Steps

1. The Account A administrator user attaches a bucket policy granting cross-account permissions to Account B to perform specific bucket operations.
2. The administrator user in Account B automatically inherits the permissions granted to Account B.
3. The Account B administrator user attaches a user policy to the user, delegating the permissions it received from Account A.
4. The user in Account B verifies permissions by accessing an object in the bucket owned by Account A.

## Setup

The walkthrough does not use root user credentials. Instead, an administrator user is created in each account and used to create resources and grant permissions. Account A has AWS account ID 1111-1111-1111 and administrator user AccountAadmin. Account B has AWS account ID 2222-2222-2222 and administrator user AccountBadmin.

Creating users and granting permissions is done in the AWS Management Console. Permissions are verified using the AWS CLI or AWS Tools for Windows PowerShell, so no code needs to be written. AccountAadmin is granted administrator privileges by attaching a user policy giving full access. All users in an account must use the account's IAM user sign-in URL when signing in to the AWS Management Console. With the AWS CLI, two profiles, AccountAadmin and AccountBadmin, are created for the administrator users' credentials.

## Step 1: Account A Grants Permissions

AccountAadmin signs in to the console, creates the bucket amzn-s3-demo-bucket, and attaches a policy to it. The bucket policy grants Account B the s3:GetLifecycleConfiguration and s3:ListBucket permissions on amzn-s3-demo-bucket. After the bucket policy is attached, Account B (and thus its administrator user) can perform s3:ListBucket and s3:GetLifecycleConfiguration on the bucket.

## Step 2: Account B Delegates to a User

The Account B administrator creates user Dave in Account B. An inline policy attached to Dave allows only the s3:ListBucket action on amzn-s3-demo-bucket.

## Step 3: Verify Permissions

Dave in Account B can list the contents of amzn-s3-demo-bucket owned by Account A. Dave doesn't have any permissions other than s3:ListBucket, so if Dave tries get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration, Amazon S3 returns permission denied.

## Step 4: Explicit Deny

Because an explicit deny takes precedence over any other permissions, if the bucket policy explicitly denies Account B the s3:ListBucket permission, Account B and users in Account B will not be able to list objects in amzn-s3-demo-bucket. After the explicit deny policy replaces the bucket policy, AccountBadmin's attempt to get a bucket list is denied access.

## Cleanup

Remove the bucket policy from amzn-s3-demo-bucket. If the bucket was created for this exercise, delete the objects and then the bucket. Finally, delete the AccountAadmin and AccountBadmin users.

## Background

Granting permissions to IAM roles is a better practice than granting permissions to individual users. This walkthrough nonetheless uses users to show the mechanics of cross-account access.

A user in Account B still needs permission from the parent account, Account B, even if Account B doesn't have permissions from Account A. The user will be able to access the resource only when both of these hold: the resource owner has granted the permission (directly via bucket policy), and the parent account has granted it too. As long as the user has permission from both the resource owner and the parent account, the user will be able to access the resource.

The Account A administrator user attaches a bucket policy granting cross-account permissions to Account B to perform specific bucket operations. Because that policy is attached, the administrator user in Account B automatically inherits the permissions granted to Account B. The Account B administrator user then attaches a user policy to the user, delegating the permissions it received from Account A. Finally, the user in Account B verifies permissions by accessing an object in the bucket owned by Account A.

The walkthrough does not use root user credentials. Instead, an administrator user is created in each account and used to create resources and grant permissions. Account A has AWS account ID 1111-1111-1111 and administrator user AccountAadmin. Account B has AWS account ID 2222-2222-2222 and administrator user AccountBadmin.

Creating users and granting permissions is done in the AWS Management Console. Permissions are verified using the AWS CLI or AWS Tools for Windows PowerShell, so no code needs to be written.
